title: Casetext CoCounsel launch releases (March 2023): unveiling and GPT-4 disclosure
author: Casetext

dom.t: Legal agents: Connected matter work retains review

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: Casetext treats bar-exam performance as validation of professional-grade legal AI and predicts transformative change without deployment-specific, task-level evidence. This conflicts with the cluster’s emphasis on multidisciplinary implementation, substantive verification and real-workflow evaluation over exam success or model demonstrations.
qs: Casetext also confirms that GPT-4 has passed both the multiple-choice and written portions of the Uniform Bar Exam (UBE), a first for this technology.
GPT-4's advanced reasoning—validated by its performance on the bar—has unlocked professional-grade AI for law, ushering in an era of rapid and profound change in the legal industry.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Casetext shifts the focus from bounded, supervised workflow gains and competence risks to a promotional capability claim: it treats GPT-4’s bar-exam performance as validation of professional-grade legal AI and predicts rapid industry transformation. This materially departs from the cluster’s warning that benchmark success does not establish competence across legal practice, while offering no evidence on verification, user capability or apprenticeship risk.
qs: Casetext also confirms that GPT-4 has passed both the multiple-choice and written portions of the Uniform Bar Exam (UBE), a first for this technology.
GPT-4's advanced reasoning—validated by its performance on the bar—has unlocked professional-grade AI for law, ushering in an era of rapid and profound change in the legal industry.

st.t: Legal agents: Connected matter work retains review
st.an: Casetext supports the shift toward delegating substantive legal tasks to an AI assistant and supplies development, adoption and privacy claims. But it goes beyond the cluster’s cautious conclusion by asserting that lawyers can trust CoCounsel’s results, despite offering no comparative legal-work performance evidence and not clearly foregrounding lawyer review.
qs: For the first time, lawyers can reliably delegate substantive, complex work to an AI assistant—just as they would to a legal professional—and trust the results.

Casetext's Trust Team, which has run every legal skill on the platform through thousands of internal tests, has spent nearly 4,000 hours training and fine-tuning CoCounsel's output based on over 30,000 legal questions.

kp.k: CoCounsel promises delegation of substantive legal tasks
kp.d: In its 1 March 2023 launch release, Casetext presents CoCounsel as an assistant to which lawyers can delegate legal research, document review, deposition preparation and contract analysis. CEO Jake Heller frames the change as freeing attorneys for more impactful work. The release goes beyond a productivity claim to assert that lawyers can trust delegated complex work; this is Casetext's product claim.
qs: It creates a momentous opportunity for attorneys to delegate tasks like legal research, document review, deposition preparation, and contract analysis to an AI, freeing them to focus on the most impactful aspects of their practice.
For the first time, lawyers can reliably delegate substantive, complex work to an AI assistant—just as they would to a legal professional—and trust the results.

kp.k: Legal databases and search underpin claimed professional reliability
kp.d: Casetext distinguishes CoCounsel from general-purpose public language models by describing its combination of OpenAI technology, proprietary legal databases and Parallel Search. It attributes faster, more accurate substantive legal work and professional usability to this legal-specific configuration.
qs: In building CoCounsel, Casetext has coupled the immense technological power of OpenAI's most advanced model with its own proprietary legal databases and market-leading legal search system, Parallel Search.
As a result, CoCounsel can perform substantive tasks such as legal research, document review, deposition preparation, and contract analysis more quickly and accurately than ever before possible.

kp.k: Launch reliability claims cite extensive testing and practitioner use
kp.d: Casetext reports a trust program staffed by AI engineers and experienced litigation and transactional attorneys: thousands of internal tests for every legal skill, nearly 4,000 hours training and fine-tuning output based on over 30,000 legal questions, and extensive pre-deployment beta use by over 400 attorneys from firms, in-house departments and legal aid organizations. It reports more than 50,000 uses in daily work. These are reported testing and usage volumes rather than quantified accuracy results.
qs: Casetext's Trust Team, which has run every legal skill on the platform through thousands of internal tests, has spent nearly 4,000 hours training and fine-tuning CoCounsel's output based on over 30,000 legal questions.

Then, all CoCounsel applications were used extensively by a group of beta testers composed of over 400 attorneys from elite boutique and global law firms, in-house legal departments, and legal aid organizations, before being deployed.
These lawyers and legal professionals have already used CoCounsel more than 50,000 times in their day-to-day work.

kp.k: Early law-firm adopters report efficiency and client benefits
kp.d: The first release identifies Fisher Phillips as the first major firm to deploy CoCounsel firm-wide to its 500+ attorneys. Its chairman and managing partner John Polson reports immediate, sustained client benefits from research, review, drafting and summarizing. Bowman and Brooke's Chris Austin attributes greater attorney agility and precision to beta use. These are customer testimonials carried by Casetext.
qs: John Polson, Chairman and Managing Partner of Fisher Phillips, the first major law firm to deploy CoCounsel firm-wide to its 500+ attorneys.

The power of this tool to help our attorneys perform efficient legal research, document review, drafting, and summarizing, has already resulted in immediate, sustained benefits to our clients, and we have only scratched the surface of what it has to offer.
CoCounsel doesn't just eliminate essential yet time-consuming work, it enables our attorneys to become more agile and precise—it's changing how we practice law for the better.

kp.k: GPT-4 disclosure links bar performance to professional capability
kp.d: On 14 March 2023, Casetext identifies GPT-4 as CoCounsel's underlying model and reports a collaboration with Dan Katz and Michael Bommarito from Stanford's Center for Legal Informatics. According to the release's account of their forthcoming paper, GPT-4 passed the UBE multiple-choice portion and both written components, exceeding earlier models and the average real-life test-taker score; an earlier model released in late 2022 had passed no portion. Casetext interprets this performance as validating reasoning capable of enabling professional-grade legal AI.
qs: Legal AI company Casetext announced that its AI legal assistant, CoCounsel, is powered by GPT-4, the latest, most advanced large language model from OpenAI, released today.
Katz and Bommarito had earlier examined the performance of a large language model released in late 2022, finding it could not pass any portion of the UBE.

Their forthcoming paper shows that GPT-4, however, passed the multiple-choice portion and both components of the written portion, exceeding not only all prior large language models' scores, but also the average score of real-life bar exam test takers.
GPT-4's advanced reasoning—validated by its performance on the bar—has unlocked professional-grade AI for law, ushering in an era of rapid and profound change in the legal industry.

kp.k: Confidentiality protections are presented as prerequisites for legal adoption
kp.d: Both releases emphasize security and confidentiality as distinguishing professional legal AI from generalized models. CTO Ryan Walker specifically asserts that client data is never used to train models and that law firms retain complete control over their data.
qs: Unlike generalized, publicly available large language models, CoCounsel is a product that offers the reliability and security critical for legal matters, which are specialized, complex, and confidential.
Client data is never used to train the models, and law firms retain complete control over their data.

kp.k: DLA Piper frames adoption as a competitive necessity
kp.d: The second release reports early access among selected Fortune 50 and Am Law 50 clients and says DLA Piper had used CoCounsel since September 2022. DLA Piper Americas Chair Frank Ryan describes automation as freeing lawyers for higher-impact practice and presents timely AI adoption as important to business growth and competition.
qs: Global law firm and Casetext client DLA Piper received early access to CoCounsel and has been using the AI assistant since September 2022.
Casetext's CoCounsel is changing how the law is practiced by automating critical, time-intensive tasks and freeing our lawyers to focus on the most impactful aspects of practice
AI development and adoption is crucial as companies look to grow their businesses and compete successfully. No firm wants to be the last one to implement this game-changing technology.

kp.k: Faster legal analysis supports refugee class-action work
kp.d: Immigration attorney and beta customer Greg Siskind reports using CoCounsel in a class action for Ukrainian refugees allegedly improperly charged millions of dollars in illegal fees. His specific reported benefit is faster vetting of a foundational legal theory, illustrating the release's claim that AI can expand lawyers' practical capacity.
qs: We are working on a class action case on behalf of Ukrainian refugees who were improperly charged millions of dollars in illegal fees.
CoCounsel has been instrumental in supporting us. It was able to expedite the vetting process of a legal theory that is foundational to our arguments at superhuman speed.

kp.k: Legal-aid capacity gains and justice benefits remain differently qualified
kp.d: Casetext asserts that CoCounsel already enables legal aid lawyers to help more people across more matters despite resource constraints. Ford's Darth Vaughn reports emerging value across practice groups but makes increased access to justice conditional on correct implementation. California Innocence Project managing attorney Michael Semanchik describes current assistance in addressing resource disparities in wrongful-conviction work and potential future benefits for defense attorneys and public defenders.
qs: Legal aid work is critical to expanding access to justice, but time and resource constraints commonly limit impact.
CoCounsel is already empowering legal aid lawyers to serve more people in need across a broader range of legal matters.
The value of CoCounsel is quickly becoming evident across a range of our practice groups. If implemented correctly, I believe this technology can also increase access to justice.

Providing access to CoCounsel certainly helps us to level that playing field on the back end. Access to CoCounsel on the front end could help defense attorneys and public defenders level the playing field as well.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Casetext claims CoCounsel enables reliable delegation of substantive legal tasks, increasing speed and accuracy and freeing lawyers for higher-impact work.
pts.d: The March 1 release presents legal research, document review, deposition preparation and contract analysis as tasks lawyers can delegate to CoCounsel. CEO Jake Heller frames the change as freeing attorneys to concentrate on the most impactful parts of practice. Casetext further claims the resulting capacity lets attorneys undertake projects otherwise impossible. This is a lawyer-facing delegation and augmentation claim, not an explicit prediction of lawyer replacement; the releases do not specify human verification requirements.

pts.k: Named law-firm users describe already-realized efficiency, client benefits and changes to legal practice.
pts.d: Fisher Phillips chairman and managing partner John Polson reports immediate, sustained client benefits from research, review, drafting and summarizing. Bowman and Brooke's Chris Austin says the tool removes time-consuming work and makes attorneys more agile and precise. Orrick's Wendy Butler Curtis reports existing added value while treating further integration as exploratory. DLA Piper Americas Chair Frank Ryan attributes a change in practice to task automation and predicts competitive pressure to adopt AI.

pts.k: Casetext presents GPT-4's reasoning and legal customization as enabling professional-grade AI and rapid industry change.
pts.d: The March 14 release identifies GPT-4 as CoCounsel's underlying model and treats its reported bar-exam performance as validation of advanced reasoning. Casetext co-founder Pablo Arredondo emphasizes interpretation rather than text generation alone. Casetext attributes professional reliability to combining the model with legal expertise, proprietary databases and Parallel Search. CTO Ryan Walker claims client data is not used for model training, firms retain data control, and CoCounsel is the most secure AI in legal technology.

pts.k: Casetext and users claim greater legal-service capacity can expand access to justice, with conditional predictions for wider benefits.
pts.d: Casetext says CoCounsel already enables legal aid lawyers to assist more people across more matters. Ford's Darth Vaughn predicts increased access to justice if implementation is correct. California Innocence Project managing attorney Michael Semanchik reports resource-equalizing benefits in post-conviction work and suggests similar potential for defense attorneys and public defenders earlier in proceedings. These criminal-defense examples are distinct from the release's broader legal-aid and civil-access claims. Immigration lawyer Greg Siskind describes accelerated legal-theory vetting in litigation for Ukrainian refugees.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Casetext supports reliability claims with reported internal testing and beta-use volumes.
pts.d: The March 1 release reports thousands of internal tests for every legal skill, nearly 4,000 hours of training and fine-tuning based on over 30,000 legal questions, over 400 attorney beta testers, and more than 50,000 uses in daily work. These are development and usage counts offered by the vendor, not reported accuracy rates or quantified task-level productivity results. Beta testers span law firms, in-house departments and legal aid organizations. The described testing concerns product development rather than users' verification of individual outputs.

pts.k: The March 14 release offers a forthcoming GPT-4 bar-exam study as evidence of model capability.
pts.d: Casetext reports collaborating with Dan Katz and Michael Bommarito, identified in the release as researchers from Stanford's Center for Legal Informatics. It says GPT-4 passed the multiple-choice and both written components of the UBE and exceeded the average real-life test-taker score, whereas an earlier model examined by the researchers passed no portion. No numerical scores or study methods are supplied in the releases. The reported benchmark concerns GPT-4's exam performance, while the professional-practice implications are claims Casetext draws from it.

pts.k: Practice benefits and access claims are supported by customer testimony, deployment examples and a specific litigation anecdote.
pts.d: The releases cite Fisher Phillips's firm-wide deployment to more than 500 attorneys and DLA Piper's use since September 2022. Siskind describes assistance with a class action concerning allegedly illegal fees charged to Ukrainian refugees; Semanchik offers experience from innocence work. These accounts do not include measured time savings, additional-client counts or case outcomes. Security claims are attributed to Casetext's CTO without a comparative security study. The stated customer base of over 10,000 firms concerns Casetext generally, not CoCounsel-specific adoption.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The releases portray benefits as present by March 2023, with broader transformation imminent but undated and dependent on implementation and legal specialization.
pts.d: CoCounsel is unveiled on March 1; GPT-4 is identified publicly on March 14. Reported benefits draw on prior beta use, including DLA Piper's use since September 2022. Casetext describes rapid industry change without a specific forecast horizon. Reliability is framed as a consequence of combining GPT-4 with legal expertise, databases, search, security and testing, rather than using a generalized public model alone. Vaughn explicitly conditions access-to-justice benefits on correct implementation; Semanchik's front-end defense benefits remain prospective.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects span provider-side lawyers, corporate legal departments, clients and resource-constrained people needing representation.
pts.d: Law-firm attorneys are said to gain capacity, precision and time for higher-impact work; firms face competitive incentives to adopt. Named deployments and beta participants include major global firms and boutiques. In-house departments, Fortune 50 clients and Ford practice groups are presented as beneficiaries of improved workflows. Clients are said to receive more efficient and higher-quality representation. Legal aid lawyers may serve more people and more types of matters; refugees, wrongfully convicted people and criminal defendants feature as public beneficiaries. Casetext is the software vendor in these accounts, not an ALSP delivering legal work. The releases make no concrete predictions about staffing reductions, junior-lawyer employment or fee-model changes.
